items.title: US officials visit Palestinian village after settler attacks on diplomats
items.author: Ali Sawafta, Steven Scheer
items.creator: Ali Sawafta, Steven Scheer
items.summary: While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack, Benjamin Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, has been more circumspect.
items.body:
US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on [USN:L1N46305Z TEXT:"European diplomats"] and an [USN:L1N4620BI TEXT:"American photojournalist"] in the previous two days.
Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.
Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians, had been attacked near Taybeh on Saturday by masked Israeli settlers.
The previous day, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was taken to hospital after being assaulted while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near another West Bank village.
The diplomats' visit coincided with US President Donald Trump [USN:L1N46403J TEXT:"endorsing"] his ally, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for Israel's parliamentary election on October 27.
Meanwhile, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee attended a settler conference in the West Bank on Sunday.
Huckabee, an evangelical Christian and longtime supporter of Israel, earlier wrote on X calling for "those who attacked" the Washington Post photojournalist, a US citizen, to be jailed.
NETANYAHU CIRCUMSPECT ON SETTLER VIOLENCE Trump has expressed his opposition to Israeli annexation of the West Bank, but his administration has put little [USN:L6N45G09W TEXT:"pressure on Netanyahu's"] right-wing, pro-settler government to change its policy.
UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law, but Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military both blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats, Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, has been more circumspect.
He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" with the Israeli military, and that the facts of the attack on Levine are "unclear".
France urged Israeli authorities to arrest Saturday's attackers and to end criminal violence in the West Bank, but by Sunday there was no announcement from Israeli authorities of any arrests in either of the two latest incidents.
The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.
Yet prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.
On Sunday, Reuters saw a group of at least 10 settlers, masked and dressed in black, hurling rocks at Palestinians and activists harvesting olives near the Palestinian West Bank town of Salfit, prompting the farmers to flee.
Israeli border police were in the area and shot tear gas towards the hills.

items.title: Arsenal edge Forest with late goal, Man United held by Leeds
items.author: Lori Ewing
items.creator: Lori Ewing
items.summary: Champions Arsenal needed a late goal from Noni Madueke, their only shot on target, to scrape a 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest and remain three points behind Premier League leaders Manchester City.
items.body:
Champions Arsenal needed a late goal from Noni Madueke, their only shot on target, to scrape a 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest on Sunday and remain three points behind Premier League leaders Manchester City.
Brighton & Hove Albion's Diego Gomez struck a sensational goal from inside his own half in a 5-0 rout of Crystal Palace on Sunday to leave his side third in the table with 16 points, five behind leaders Manchester City.
Manchester United and bitter rivals Leeds United shared the spoils in a 1-1 draw at Elland Road at the end of a turbulent week for the Red Devils in which defender Lisandro Martinez had publicly challenged the club's hierarchy.
Leeds are seventh in the table and Manchester United, who have just one win from seven games, are 13th.
Bournemouth beat Sunderland 2-0 for their first league victory of the season to climb to 15th place. Sunderland remained in the drop zone in 19th place.
At the City Ground, a frustrated Arsenal finally sealed victory in the 80th minute.
Ibrahim Sangare hesitated when he could have cleared the ball, leaving Forest manager Oliver Glasner visibly fuming, and second-half substitute Madueke then danced past Daniel Munoz before hammering a shot that deflected off Jair Cunha and wrong-footed Matz Sels.
"We're really happy, we did it all together. We showed grit, determination, and maybe we showed a champion spirit here for that, really pleased," Madueke told Sky Sports.
Murillo almost salvaged a point for Forest in injury time when he beat three players before unleashing a shot that sailed agonisingly wide.
The defeat left Forest, who have yet to win or even score at the City Ground this season, in the drop zone in 18th place with five points.
At the Amex, Brighton got on the scoresheet in the fourth minute through a Jaydee Canvot own goal, before Gomez struck a goal of the season contender three minutes later, robbing Adam Wharton of the ball near the halfway line before taking a touch and firing the ball over keeper Walter Benitez and into the net.
"When I got the ball I knew the goalkeeper was a little bit ahead," Gomez told Sky Sports. "When I scored I didn't know where to run or what to do. I was very happy with the goal."
Yasin Ayari padded Brighton's lead three minutes later, before Charalampos Kostoulas and Jack Hinshelwood completed the rout after the break.
Kostoulas scored just after halftime when Ayari's shot deflected into the Greece international's path, and Hinshelwood struck in the 84th when Luka Vuskovic's header was scooped off the line by Benitez and he fired home the rebound.
MBEUMO GRABS OPENING GOAL Manchester United looked on course for a much-needed victory when Bryan Mbeumo scored in the 35th minute after missing a couple of chances. Mbeumo held off James Justin before tapping in a Youri Tielemans cross from six yards out.
Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised in the 51st minute, chesting down the ball from a corner before poking home.
"We are slightly disappointed it is just a point," Leeds boss Daniel Farke told Sky. "Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance.
"We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester United."
Manchester defender Martinez retained his place in Michael Carrick's starting lineup despite criticising United's hierarchy following Tuesday's 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, questioning the club’s summer investment and singling out director of football Jason Wilcox before later apologising.
Bournemouth punished a shaky Sunderland start to take the lead after just six minutes, when Lewis Cook lofted a long ball forward that Evanilson ran on to and squared for Marcus Tavernier to head home from close range.
Evanilson scored himself in the 48th minute when the Brazilian rounded goalkeeper Robin Roefs before slotting home left-footed.

items.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu in close Israeli election
items.author: Doina Chiacu, Alexander Cornwell
items.creator: Doina Chiacu, Alexander Cornwell
items.summary: The endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the October 27 national election.
items.body:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week's parliamentary election.
Trump praised Netanyahu as a "great warrior prime minister" and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February. The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilizing regional economies.
"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
"Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure — But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today."
In his message, addressed to "the Great People of Israel," Trump added, "Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel."
The Trump endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the October 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.
Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel's prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote.
It will be Israel's first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.
Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to his "dear friend Donald" on X, saying, "Together we will complete the mission!"
Trump has broken with longtime US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras.
ENDORSEMENT MIGHT HELP, CAN'T HURT Trump's relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticizing Israel's longest-serving prime minister.
The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, who vote November 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel's conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.
Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump's late endorsement could help win back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.
Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favor of the Iran war.
In an election this close, "it couldn't hurt him, and it might help," said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.
Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister while another election is held.
The US president passed up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.
"However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision," Miller added.
A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised "legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done," he said.

items.title: Huracán Trudy se debilita frente a costa del Pacífico mexicano, comienzan labores de limpieza
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: El huracán Trudy se debilitaba el domingo frente a la costa del Pacífico mexicano mientras se alejaba del continente, informaron autoridades meteorológicas de México y Estados Unidos.
items.body:
El huracán Trudy se debilitaba el domingo frente a la costa del Pacífico mexicano mientras se alejaba del continente, informaron autoridades meteorológicas de México y Estados Unidos.
El Centro Nacional de Huracanes estadounidense (NHC, por sus siglas en inglés) dijo en su reporte más reciente que Trudy se ubicaba a unos 290 kilómetros al oeste-noroeste de Manzanillo, con vientos máximos sostenidos de 155 kilómetros por hora (km/h), y avanzaba hacia el noroeste a 9 km/h.
Se esperaba que el centro de Trudy se alejara aún más de la costa mexicana antes de pasar cerca del sur de Baja California Sur entre el lunes y el martes. El Gobierno de México levantó todas las alertas por huracán y tormenta tropical a lo largo de la costa del Pacífico y en el archipiélago de las Islas Marías.
Sin embargo, las autoridades recomendaron mantener vigilancia preventiva en el suroeste y centro-oeste del país, así como en Baja California Sur. Por otra parte, las autoridades advirtieron sobre condiciones meteorológicas severas asociadas con el frente frío número 2 en el sur y sureste del país.
La Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil dijo que se esperaba que el sistema permaneciera estacionario sobre el sur del estado Veracruz, con potencial de provocar lluvias extraordinarias y torrenciales. Añadió que mantendría una estrecha vigilancia sobre los niveles de ríos y embalses de ese estado además de Tabasco, Chiapas y Oaxaca.
Los fuertes vientos del norte y oleaje de hasta seis metros ya habían provocado inundaciones en zonas costeras y cierres de carreteras en algunas zonas de Tabasco.
En Veracruz, más de 1,500 viviendas resultaron afectadas por inundaciones, mientras las autoridades realizaban labores de limpieza y recuperación a medida que descendían gradualmente los niveles del agua.
En las últimas semanas, la costa del Pacífico mexicano ha sido afectada por los huracanes [USN:L6N45L0YK TEXT:"Polo y Simon"], así como por la tormenta Rachel. Las inundaciones dejaron al menos ocho muertos en la ciudad costera de Ensenada, en el estado de Baja California.

Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday (Oct 18), as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on authorizing the request for military support on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.

"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed Salman, who visited Sisi on Sep 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of President Mohamed Morsi in 2013.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

items.title: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shoot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said.
items.body:
Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Sunday the drones were likely latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.
"The ones from last night were flying at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop engine," Miruta said. "This is the first time we've shot down drones like these."
The drones were [USN:L8N4610EC TEXT:"brought down"] days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO's eastern flank.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.
NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Romania started [USN:L8N43Q0KW TEXT:"shooting down drones"] that enter its space earlier this year.
The defence ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively.
"NATO is ready and able to react to any potential threat, 24/7, to safeguard our territory and protect our people," a NATO official told Reuters.
Romania's Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said the North Atlantic Council will have a meeting on Tuesday to discuss Black Sea defence and deterrence.
The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still [USN:L8N4620JP TEXT:"searching"] for seven missing crew members.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters.
In Moldova, on Romania's northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone's origin.
Five drones identified as Russian [USN:L1N46210E TEXT:"fell on Moldovan territory"] in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions.

items.title: US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelenskiy says
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said intelligence-sharing was interrupted and later "de-blocked."
items.body:
The United States has resumed providing Ukraine critical intelligence to help it defend against Russian missile strikes, after a brief pause, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in comments published on Sunday.
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to spot the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities. US President Donald Trump had [USN:L1N45Z16F TEXT:"said earlier this week"] that Washington was still sharing intelligence, although Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning.
Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked."
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
But Zelenskiy said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and [USN:L6N464042 TEXT:"waiving sanctions on Russia"] that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine.
"If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand," he said.
Over the past week, a [USN:L6N46303A TEXT:"widening rift"] between Trump and Zelenskiy has sparked concerns that their tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Zelenskiy told NBC that he hopes Trump will remain an ally of Ukraine.
"We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions," Zelenskiy said. "Because I think that it's all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States."
In a Truth Social post on Sunday afternoon, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."
Ukraine gets US help that Russia does not receive, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told NBC, citing intelligence-sharing and the provision of US munitions to other countries for resale to Ukraine.
But Bessent, speaking with "Meet the Press" after it aired Zelenskiy's interview, did not directly answer when asked multiple times whether the United States views Ukraine as an ally.
"Zelenskiy presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win," Bessent said. "The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement."

items.title: Hurricane Trudy weakens off Mexico's Pacific coast as cleanup effort begins
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Hurricane Trudy weakened slightly off Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday and was expected to begin rapidly losing strength later in the day as it moved away from the mainland, forecasters said.
items.body:
Hurricane Trudy weakened slightly off Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday and was expected to begin rapidly losing strength later in the day as it moved away from the mainland, forecasters said.
The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Trudy was located about 180 miles (290 km) west-northwest of Manzanillo, with maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (155 kph), down from 105 mph earlier in the day, moving northwest at 6 mph (9 kph).
Trudy's center is expected to move farther away from Mexico's Pacific coast before passing south of Baja California Sur on Monday and Tuesday.
Mexico's government, meanwhile, discontinued all hurricane and tropical storm warnings along the Pacific coast and for the Islas Marias archipelago, but authorities said locals in southwestern and west-central Mexico, as well as Baja California Sur, should continue to monitor the storm.
Separately, Mexican authorities warned of severe weather linked to Cold Front No. 2 in the country's south and southeast. The National Civil Protection Coordination said the system was expected to stall over southern Veracruz, bringing extraordinary and torrential rainfall.
In Veracruz, more than 1,500 homes were affected by floodwaters, while federal, state and municipal authorities were carrying out cleanup and recovery operations as water levels gradually receded.
Civil protection authorities also said they were closely monitoring river and reservoir levels in Veracruz, Tabasco, Chiapas and Oaxaca, while strong northerly winds and waves of up to 6 meters (20 feet) had already caused coastal flooding and road closures in parts of Tabasco.

SEOUL, Oct 18 : Samsung Electronics will use TSMC's 3-nanometre process to produce base dies for Nvidia's next-generation custom high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, the Seoul Economic Daily reported on Sunday.
The move would mark the first time Samsung has worked with the Taiwanese contract chipmaker at the HBM manufacturing stage, according to the report.
• Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology to use TSMC's process for NVHBM base dies, and sixth-generation DRAM technology for its core dies, the newspaper said, citing industry sources.
• NVHBM, unveiled in August, integrates Nvidia's custom memory controller into the base die and is aimed at standardising implementation across multiple memory suppliers, according to the company.

items.title: IMF/World Bank meetings leave developing countries with more questions than answers
items.author: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
items.creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
items.summary: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
items.body:
Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
Not for the first time, [USN:L1N46302K TEXT:"lower-income countries"] are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom.
What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment.
Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs.
Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said.
ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI:
"We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you."
Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help.
"It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment."
Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future.
"The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold."
The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an [USN:L1N46301V TEXT:"IMF steering committee"] walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight.
And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector.
RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms.
"If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged.”
Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected.
But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before.
Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%.
“People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock."
While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022.
Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries.
“The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

items.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
items.body:
Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an [USN:L1N42P0Q6 TEXT:"interim ceasefire"] collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but [USN:L1N45X04L TEXT:"Iran’s security chief"] said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all [USN:L1N45Q01J TEXT:"seven conditions"] for reopening the strait.
"Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.
If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] from the outset.
US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

items.title: Accenture looks to sell Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, FT reports
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: IT consulting firm Accenture is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
items.body:
IT consulting firm Accenture (ACN.N) is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Accenture has hired JPMorgan (JPM.N) to work on a strategic review of the China business after receiving unsolicited interest in the unit over the past year, the report added.
Accenture and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment outside regular business hours.
The sale process is likely to draw interest from private equity groups and a small cluster of strategic buyers, the report said.
Accenture may opt to retain a significant minority stake in the business, the report added.
Accenture’s Greater China operations include Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China, according to its website.
The consultancy firm recently forecast full-year 2027 revenue growth between 3% and 6%, above analysts' estimates.

items.title: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
items.author: Joshua McElwee
items.creator: Joshua McElwee
items.summary: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
items.body:
Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an [USN:S8N42Y05U TEXT:"operation"] on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"fuelling speculation"] about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Smiling from a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.
"Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Leo said.
The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.
He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise".
NUN CRIES AS LEO MAKES APPEARANCE Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock.
His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough to return home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.
Crowds in St. Peter's Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face.
A few steps away, a group of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, "Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you".
POPE'S CALENDAR IN FLUX Leo usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square. It has not said whether he will hold that audience.
The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"].
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, has however expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health".
items.raw_description: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.

items.title: Roy Cooper's North Carolina playbook is working. Can other Democrats copy it?
items.author: Yasmeen Abutaleb
items.creator: Yasmeen Abutaleb
items.summary: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper, who hasn't lost an election in four decades, has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley.
items.body:
North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley by relentlessly focusing on affordability and a blunt promise to “make stuff cost less.”
At campaign stops, Cooper, 69, points to his six-year fight to expand Medicaid through a Republican-controlled legislature as evidence he can work across party lines, while attacking Trump-backed healthcare cuts that he says are hitting North Carolinians hard.
“People should not have to make a choice between going to a doctor and putting food on the table,” Cooper said at a September 26 rally in Raleigh, North Carolina. “This 'Big Beautiful Bill' that gave tax cuts to billionaires has now driven healthcare premiums up more than double for people.”
The White House says the bill cuts taxes, protects Medicaid for eligible Americans and curbs fraud and abuse.
Cooper's message appears to be working: His lead stood at 14 points in an October SurveyUSA poll. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans has paused TV advertising in North Carolina less than three weeks before the election and begun shifting campaign dollars to defend seats in states that include Iowa and Kansas.
President Donald Trump will rally in the state on Tuesday for Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who has never held elected office.
The question for Democrats is whether Cooper's playbook can help them win Republican and independent voters elsewhere, or whether his success is unique to a popular former governor who has never lost an election in four decades of public service.
While some Democrats in heavily Democratic states have embraced Medicare for All, which would provide government-run health insurance for all Americans, Cooper has focused on expanding existing coverage and lowering costs. He points to his fight to expand Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and campaigns on prescription drug and insurance costs.
'OUR STAR ATHLETE AND NO ONE'S PAYING ANY ATTENTION' “It’s like he’s our star athlete and no one’s paying any attention,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, and former White House adviser to President Joe Biden. “The strength of Roy Cooper’s campaign is that he’s able to attract Democrats and independents, but also even some Republicans because he’s focused on cost, but he also has a record.”
Paul Shumaker, a longtime Republican strategist in North Carolina, attributes Cooper’s success to the fact he was already well-known and that Whatley failed to distinguish himself from Trump.
“Roy Cooper came to the US Senate race with a known brand that has been trusted by a majority of North Carolina voters election after election,” Shumaker said. “Republicans are suffering from a lack of trust on the economy right now and Whatley has failed to reestablish that trust.”
Cooper declined an interview request for this story. The Whatley campaign did not respond to a request for comment, but on Sunday he predicted victory during an interview with Fox News.
Trump's upcoming visit to North Carolina and an expected rally with Vice President JD Vance will energize Republican voters, Whatley told Fox News' "Sunday Briefing."
"Our election is going to come down to turnout and we're in a state that President Trump won three straight times," Whatley said.
WINNING OVER INDEPENDENTS North Carolina’s electorate is unusually independent: 40% of registered voters are unaffiliated with either party, compared with 30% each for Republicans and Democrats. Republicans, however, have dominated the state legislature for more than a decade and redrawn districts to strengthen their grip.
Like other Republican candidates, Whatley must contend with Trump’s record-low approval rating, which now hovers at 32%, according to an October [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. That poll also showed registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans nationally by 44% to 37%. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent voters still undecided.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to control the chamber — an already difficult task that makes Cooper's North Carolina race especially important.
Cooper's signature bipartisan achievement did not come easily. It took him six years to persuade the Republican-controlled state legislature to pass an expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare in 2023, extending health insurance to more than 700,000 state residents, according to state health department data. After passage, he called it “an unnecessarily long and agonizing journey.”
Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster, said several moderate Democratic governors in the South could replicate Cooper’s success, including Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear.
“The Roy Coopers of the world are not unique,” Ayres said. “The Republicans nominated someone who’s never been elected to any public office at any level anywhere running against a reasonably moderate, popular governor.”
RUNNING AGAINST HEALTHCARE CUTS Many of the state’s Medicaid gains are likely to be undone by Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a sweeping tax and budget bill the Republican-led Congress passed last year that cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, the largest cut in the program’s history, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office.
Cooper has used Trump’s signature domestic legislative achievement to paint the president and Republicans as depriving North Carolinians of healthcare in order to give billionaires more tax cuts.
He has also focused on congressional Republicans’ decision to curtail COVID-era Obamacare subsidies last year, causing healthcare premiums on the individual health insurance marketplace to spike and more than 200,000 state residents to drop their coverage, according to health policy research firm KFF.
“Roy Cooper has always polled over Republicans,” said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. “This will be the average election for Roy Cooper.”

items.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK data center deal with Nscale, Telegraph reports
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Microsoft has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday.
items.body:
Microsoft (MSFT.O) has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday.
The US tech giant, one of Nscale's two largest customers, recently terminated its agreement for the data center in Loughton, Essex, according to the report.
The newspaper did not specify why Microsoft withdrew from the project. Microsoft declined a Reuters request for comment.
The Telegraph report said Nscale had faced repeated delays with the project. National power grid officials, it reported, had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the data center until the 2030s.
"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," an Nscale spokesperson told Reuters.
"We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK."
Nscale filed for an [USN:L4N45A197 TEXT:"initial public offering"] in the US last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be its major customers, according to its prospectus.
Nscale [USN:L4N45A1JP TEXT:"provides"] infrastructure, including compute, power and data centers, as well as software for training and running AI models.
The Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) AI group, which competes against CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , Nebius (NBIS.O) , Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly since its launch, scaling from $100 million to more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.

items.title: Macron urges calm as France counts cost of worst unrest in years
items.author: Sybille de La Hamaide, Clotaire Achi, Abdul Saboor
items.creator: Sybille de La Hamaide, Clotaire Achi, Abdul Saboor
items.summary: The French president appealed for calm a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services.
items.body:
President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday, a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services.
Fresh clashes broke out in Paris and Marseille, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses.
Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.
"Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
"Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame."
Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt.
Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate grievances and their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc.
He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, as demanded by some right-wing politicians, but said the government would act to allow prefects to ban protests if necessary to protect public buildings and local businesses.
PARIS PROTESTS 'LIKE A WAR ZONE' The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting.
One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"demonstrations"] in Paris. Police made 2,400 arrests across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and protesters had set fire to piles of bicycles. A Reuters witness said there appeared to be several hundred protesters in the area.
A massive clean-up operation took place in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and from Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.
"It's like a war zone here!" exclaimed Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children and said the unrest forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique.
More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"student movement"] with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.
SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner going into next year's presidential campaign, also called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused and ransacked.
"Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France," she said in a video address.
Hard-left France Unbowed presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students.
In [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"Limoges"], famed for its porcelain, the collapse of the town hall's clock tower in a fiery blaze revived memories of the 2019 fire that devastated Paris' Notre Dame cathedral. Mayor Guillaume Guerin said not enough officers from the national police had been deployed to his city.
"There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters on Sunday. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall.
Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement.
French retailer Carrefour's (CARR.PA) CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the tens of millions of euros.

items.title: Iran's parliament approves Mehrdad Akhlaqi as minister of defence
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
items.body:
Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
Akhlaqi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.
Akhlaqi has spent decades in Iran's defence industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. He is subject to US and EU sanctions over his work in Iran's defence sector.
In a programme presented to lawmakers, Akhlaqi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate the development of defence technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies.
"If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran.
CNN reported this week that the [USN:FWN46108H TEXT:"US has developed"] strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations.
The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal.
"The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlaqi said.

items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: China's solar power equipment exports fell 6.4% in September from the same month last year, customs data showed on Sunday.
items.body:
China's solar power equipment exports fell 6.4% in September from the same month last year, customs data showed on Sunday.
China, the world's largest solar manufacturer, exported 1.21 million metric tons of solar cells and panels in September. That was down from September a year earlier but up from 840,000 tons in August.
In the year through September, China exported 9.37 million tons of the equipment, down 9.5%.
September solar exports were valued at $3.34 billion, up 19.4%.
On a per-unit basis, China shipped 11.3% more cells and panels, or 1.44 billion.

items.title: China proposes export controls on solar-manufacturing technologies
items.author: Colleen Howe
items.creator: Colleen Howe
items.summary: China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
items.body:
China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a [USN:P8N44A04L TEXT:"broader revision"] that also covers AI and biotechnology.
The ministry of commerce proposed adding the photovoltaic technologies to China's export-control list, it said in a statement on Friday, adding that greater oversight is needed because solar technologies are increasingly being used in sensitive areas like aerospace and national defense.
Chinese officials held [USN:L1N40Y0TZ TEXT:"initial talks"] with manufacturers about potential curbs on advanced solar-panel manufacturing technologies, Reuters reported in April, a move that could threaten plans by US firms such as Tesla (TSLA.O) to [USN:L6N4080PX TEXT:"expand production"] in the US.
Beijing has also curbed exports of solar-manufacturing technology to [USN:L4N43A1F4 TEXT:"India,"] Reuters has reported. Analysts say China is seeking to preserve its dominance as India tries to build up domestic manufacturing and shake off reliance on China.
Export restrictions aim to "guard against the risks of technologies from running out of control or being improperly disseminated, while safeguarding normal international exchanges and cooperation in science and technology," the ministry said.
Exporters must now register certain overseas technology transfers until the export-control catalogue is formally updated. Public consultation on the proposal will close on November 15.
China would ban technologies including those used to make some thin wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, as well as large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon production technologies.
Perovskite is an emerging technology that offers the potential of increased conversion efficiency. Tandem cells combine perovskite and silicon layers to capture more of the sunlight spectrum.
Fluidized-bed technology for producing polysilicon — a key building block for solar panels — is less expensive and more energy-efficient than the dominant Siemens process.
China would also restrict, but not prohibit, exports of advanced solar cell manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, HJT and XBC.

items.title: Lithuanians forced to take shelter after suspected drone enters airspace
items.author: Andrius Sytas
items.creator: Andrius Sytas
items.summary: Ukraine's foreign ministry said the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting its drones off course.
items.body:
A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday morning, the president and other defence officials said.
Ukraine 's Foreign Ministry [USN:L8N46404Q TEXT:"said"] later it regretted the incident in Lithuania's airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course.
The object flew into Lithuania's airspace from Poland, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters, after proposing a joint investigation to his Polish counterpart.
"Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU," Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on X.
"What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population," he added.
NATO SCRAMBLES FIGHTERS Poland's military said it was also [USN:FWN4630JH TEXT:"verifying a possible violation of its airspace"] by an unidentified object.
A Polish Defence Ministry spokesperson later said radar systems did not confirm the object crossing the border into Lithuania, but added that Polish authorities were remaining in contact with Lithuanian officials.
During the "red" alert, NATO fighter jets were scrambled to the area, and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania's second-largest city, was temporarily closed, the Lithuanian government's crisis management centre said.
The NATO aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said.
Lithuanian army personnel were investigating possible drone debris near Juodzionys village in northern Lithuania, after the object disappeared from radar, possibly after exploding, the centre said.
Some of the debris struck a civilian vehicle, Kaunas said.
"We can confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official said.
"The aircraft were operating under NATO command. An investigation is ongoing, and NATO remains in close contact with the Lithuanian authorities," the official said, adding that the alliance was ready and able to react to any potential threat.
Northern neighbour Latvia briefly issued a "yellow" air warning in some regions bordering Lithuania, citing a "possible threat", its army said.
Ukrainian drones have repeatedly [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"entered NATO airspace"] in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming.
This has stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.

items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein have signed a free-trade agreement with Vietnam, the governments of Norway and Vietnam announced on Sunday.
items.body:
Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein have signed a free-trade agreement with Vietnam, the governments of Norway and Vietnam announced on Sunday.
Vietnam's trade ministry said it signed the deal in Hanoi with the European Free Trade Association members.
Around half of Norway's exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free when the agreement enters into force, with more than 98% to be tariff-free within seven years, the Norwegian government said in a statement.
Long-stalled free-trade talks were [USN:L6N4600OA TEXT:"relaunched last year"] amid global tensions over US tariffs. [USN:L8N4340QC TEXT:"Negotiations concluded"] in July.
Vietnam's trade ministry said the Southeast Asian country mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles, machinery and equipment, electronics and components to the EFTA market and imports industrial machinery and equipment, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and raw materials for production.
Bilateral trade between Vietnam and EFTA member countries has averaged $2 billion annually, the ministry said.

items.title: Rubio arrives in Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
items.author: Gram Slattery, Simon Lewis
items.creator: Gram Slattery, Simon Lewis
items.summary: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
items.body:
While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.
Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly in September of last year.
Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state and was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.
Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots.
Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment."
Speaking to reporters before leaving Washington on Saturday, Rubio said the timing of the Uzbekistan trip was dictated in part by the availability of the various delegations. He also said that foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate issues rather than build long-term relationships.
"I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio told reporters. "You're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem or ... you're going because there's a conference."
US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM The delegation that greeted Rubio upon his arrival in Samarkand included Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, whom Rubio embraced warmly. Two women in traditional Uzbek attire presented Rubio and his wife with bouquets.
One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region were wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say.
In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows.
But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to [USN:L1N45Y0GJ TEXT:"import Russian diesel"], aimed at lowering domestic fuel prices before congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived"] all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude oil or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan.
India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia.
Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia.
A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip.
Separately, the US [USN:L1N3TQ0WH TEXT:"has talked to"] additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that potentially could continue in Samarkand.
More than 200 business executives are accompanying Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago.
The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday.

items.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
items.author: Nandita Bose, Gram Slattery
items.creator: Nandita Bose, Gram Slattery
items.summary: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says sanctions waiver will prolong war with Russia.
items.body:
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Friday's executive order [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"drew criticism"] from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
The diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week."
But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday.
“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

items.title: Saudi-led coalition says helicopter crash in Najran kills two crew members
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
items.body:
A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran.
The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident.
Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon."
Separately, the Saudi civil defence said on Sunday that six people were injured after a projectile it said was fired by Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran.
Najran has been hit by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated, with the [USN:L1N4620VJ TEXT:"Yemen conflict"] becoming another front in the US-led war with Iran .

items.title: Woodside natural gas project unit paused after Greenpeace protest off Western Australia
items.author: Samuel Mckeith
items.creator: Samuel Mckeith
items.summary: Woodside said operations remained paused on Sunday at a floating production unit, part of its $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project off the coast of Western Australia, due to a Greenpeace protest at the platform.
items.body:
Woodside (WDS.AX) said operations remained paused on Sunday at a floating production unit, part of its $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project off the coast of Western Australia, due to a Greenpeace protest at the platform.
Two activists from the environmental advocacy group slept overnight on the semi-submersible unit, located around 375 km (233 miles) off the state's northwest coast, in the [USN:L4N46300J TEXT:"protest"] that started on Saturday, Greenpeace said.
"Temporary hanging tents" were set up on the unit and the activists would "occupy the platform for as long as possible," Greenpeace said.
The group is concerned about the potential impact of Woodside's proposed Browse project on Scott Reef, a remote coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale. Woodside has said it expects no physical contact with the reef above the 75-metre (246-foot) water depth.
A Woodside spokesperson said "operations at the Scarborough FPU remain safely paused" on Sunday, a day after temporarily halting pre-commissioning activities as a result of the "unauthorised access".
Four activists on Saturday scaled the 70,000 metric ton unit, part of the 98% completed Scarborough project, and displayed banners with the message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef", according to Greenpeace.
Australian Border Force on Sunday said it had no update on the incident. It previously said it was working with federal and state agencies on a response.

items.title: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Marco Rubio said.
items.body:
The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday.
"We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff."
His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"attacked"] Palestinian civilians.
European diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said.
The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday.
Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

Kenya confirms four new Ebola cases, bringing total number to seven

The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya, where the first patient arrived from Congo on Oct 3.

Kenya confirmed four new cases of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus on Saturday (Oct 17), including three health workers who treated the country's first patient, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to seven, the health ministry said.
The other new case is a male relative of the index patient, who died. The relative had been in quarantine since Oct 6, the ministry said in a statement.
The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya, where the first patient arrived from Congo on Oct 3. But the ministry says it has traced and quarantined nearly all of his contacts and there is no evidence that the virus is spreading in the community .
The three health workers, two men and a woman aged 29, 35 and 32 respectively, managed the index case on Oct 3 and 4 and had been in quarantine since Oct 9, it said. All four new patients were already in quarantine when they developed symptoms and were diagnosed.

The second and third patients confirmed earlier are stable and responding well to supportive treatment, the ministry said. It said 128 of 130 listed contacts, or 98.5 percent, had been traced and placed in quarantine, higher than the 85 percent global benchmark it said was needed to break the chain of transmission.
Kenya's cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in Congo, the second-largest outbreak ever recorded, with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths.

Related:

Tan Kiat How on low risk of Ebola cross-border transmission to Singapore

WHO says Congo Ebola outbreak can still be brought under control within three months

Commentary: This Ebola outbreak should never have caught the world off guard

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola.
The first Kenyan case was a man who had been ill in Congo for about a month before travelling by road to Uganda and flying to Nairobi on Oct 3. He died on Oct 5. His arrival has raised concerns about screening at the Congo-Uganda border, which has been closed since May, and at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport.
Efforts to trace the remaining two contacts were ongoing, the ministry said. "The risk to the general public remains low as there is no evidence of community transmission," it said, adding that there were no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.

items.title: Egypt's Sisi says his presidency will end in 2030, outlines plan to prepare future leaders
items.author: Enas Alashray
items.creator: Enas Alashray
items.summary: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.
items.body:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.
The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general, the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme.
Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed".
He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts.
"I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said.
The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament.
[USN:L5N3GA3X9 TEXT:"Sisi"], 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030.
The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood — Egypt's first democratically elected leader — following mass protests.
He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.
